newsitem.title: USA: Conrail battle in key court test Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Conrail battle in key court test Thursday.

text.p: The railroad takeover battle for Conrail Inc. heads back to federal court Thursday in a hearing likely to set the stage for a crucial vote of the company's shareholders next week.

The hearing's outcome could give Norfolk Southern Corp. more backing in its effort to wrest Philadelphia-based Conrail from its intended merger partner, CSX Corp., or could tip the balance toward shareholder acceptance of the CSX-Conrail deal.
"The way the judge decides is going to dramatically affect the vote," said a takeover stock specialist familiar with the battle.
The hearing in U.S. District Court in Philadelphia begins at 9:00 a.m. Thursday, and is expected to last about half a day, lawyers said.

Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern is pursuing a $115-per-share, $10.3 billion bid for Conrail, which has agreed to merge with Richmond, Va.-based CSX in a cash-and-stock deal worth about $100-per-share, or $9 billion.
The primary issue in the hearing is Norfolk Southern's request that the court throw out a two-year "exclusivity period" in the CSX-Conrail merger agreement.
The provision forbids Conrail from entertaining another offer for the firm through the end of 1998.

Norfolk Southern said in court documents that this provision, if upheld, would effectively preclude Conrail shareholders from holding out for its offer when they vote on approving a key provision of the merger with CSX at a Jan. 17 company meeting.

Analysts said upholding the provision could shift shareholder votes in favour of the Conrail-CSX deal, or could lead to a long stalemate in which shareholders were unwilling to back the deal and Conrail and CSX held firm.

At the meeting, shareholders will be asked to waive a Pennsylvania law that would require CSX to pay "fair value" -- in effect, $110-per-share in cash -- for all Conrail shares once its Conrail stake exceeded 20 percent.

A $110-per-share cash tender offer to raise CSX's existing stake from 19.9 percent to 40 percent is due to close Jan. 22, but it cannot close without the waiver. CSX would buy the remaining 60 percent with common and preferred stock, making the total deal worth $100 per share.
Conrail stock was down 37.5 cents to $98.75 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Conrail and CSX argued in court documents that granting the exclusivity period was within the rights of Conrail's board, and was essential to protect the deal while it was being considered by federal regulatory authorities.
The two railroads have said approval was expected by late 1997, but could take longer.
In earlier such cases, long exclusivity periods have been used in the railroad industry, CSX said.

CSX and Conrail said the period was extended from 270 days to help obtain an improved offer from CSX, in which CSX in December raised its bid and agreed to pay the share-swap portion ahead of federal regulatory approval.
This effectively transferred from Conrail shareholders the risk that authorities would not approve the merger.

Norfolk Southern also is seeking a court declaration that the voting power of CSX's stake in Conrail has already crossed the 20 percent threshhold that triggers the "fair value" provision of the Pennsylvania law.
Norfolk Southern argued that Conrail's top executives acted "in concert" with CSX, and their shares should be counted along with CSX's in considering whether the threshold has been crossed.
CSX and Conrail, while disputing the argument, said CSX's sale last week of 85,000 Conrail shares to correct any "inadvertant" error rendered the issue irrelevant.
Norfolk Southern attorney Steven Rothschild said it was not possible to reverse the earlier action and said Conrail shareholders remained entitled to demand all-cash payments.
Traders and analysts said it was difficult to gauge the outcome of the hearing.

The judge, Donald Van Artsdalen, earlier ruled in favour of Conrail's rejection of the initial Norfolk Southern bid, but later surprised analysts by saying Conrail could not postpone the shareholder vote, absent a change in the bid, simply because it thought it could lose.
"In terms of this judge, it's kind of a draw right now. One-one is the score," said a trader.

Norfolk Southern has separately asked the federal Surface Transporation Board, which must approve any merger, to invalidate the exclusivity period on the grounds that it effectively and improperly gives CSX control over Conrail.
"A win tomorrow would be a home run for us. Failing that, there's the STB petition," Norfolk Southern spokesman Robin Chapman said.
